messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Waiter/Waitress
- Trauma Type: Stalking
- Pcl5: 58

She is 48, a South Eastern Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life working in restaurants, moving through dining rooms with the quiet efficiency of someone who has learned to read people quickly. She says that before everything happened, she liked the pace of waitressing: the clatter of dishes, the brief conversations, the predictability of a busy shift. Even after her divorce, when life felt smaller and more solitary, work gave her a structure she could trust. She knew how to keep tables moving, how to smooth over irritation with a smile, how to tuck her own feelings away until the end of the night.

The trouble begins with a regular customer at the restaurant where she works. At first, she notices only that he asks to sit in her section even when the dining room is nearly empty. He remembers small details she has mentioned in passing and repeats them back to her later, as if they mean more than they do. She tells herself he is lonely, maybe socially awkward. In her job, she is used to men misunderstanding politeness for interest. She keeps her tone neutral, her smile professional.

Then he starts waiting for her outside at closing. The first time, he says he just happened to be nearby. The second time, he offers to walk her to her car. After that, he appears at the grocery store she uses, then at the bus stop near her apartment, then outside the nail salon where she goes once a month. He comments on her schedule as though it is ordinary for him to know it. She feels a chill of disbelief each time, the mind scrambling for a harmless explanation even while her body already understands something is wrong.

She changes routes home. She parks in different places. She tells her manager, who shrugs and says some customers get attached. When she asks coworkers to walk her out, she tries to laugh it off, embarrassed by how frightened she already feels. The man begins sending messages through social media, first flattering, then aggrieved, then hostile when she does not respond. He accuses her of leading him on. He leaves flowers on her car windshield. One night she finds a note tucked under the wiper blade describing the blouse she wore that morning before work. After that, she stops sleeping properly.

She lies in bed listening for footsteps in the hallway outside her apartment, her whole body stiff, waiting. Every sound carries meaning: a car door slamming, someone pausing on the stairs, the buzz of her phone. She checks the lock three or four times, then again after turning off the light. When sleep comes, it is shallow and jagged. She wakes with her heart pounding, certain she has heard him at the door. In the morning, she is exhausted but restless, already scanning the street through the blinds before she leaves.

The stalking goes on for months. She reports it to police after he follows her from work to home and circles the block repeatedly. Even after making the report, she feels no safer. She starts to believe danger can slip through any crack in routine. She stops taking evening shifts because leaving after dark feels unbearable. At work, she startles when male customers stand too close to the service station. If someone lingers after paying the bill, she feels heat rise in her chest and has to steady her hands before picking up the tray. She begins forgetting orders, something that never used to happen. Her coworkers notice she has become jumpy and withdrawn. She notices herself standing with her back to walls, choosing tables near exits, watching reflections in windows.

Her world gets smaller. She no longer goes to the market she used to like because she saw him there once. She avoids posting photos online. She stops answering calls from unknown numbers and sometimes from known ones too, because the sound of the phone makes her stomach drop. Friends invite her out, but she often refuses, saying she is tired. It is partly true. Mostly, she cannot tolerate being visible. She describes feeling as if her life has been divided into before and after, and in the after-version she is never off duty. Even in her own apartment, she is braced.

Now, years later, the stalking has ended, but her body behaves as if it could start again at any moment. She still checks over her shoulder walking to her car after a shift. If a customer asks a personal question, she feels instant alarm and gives clipped, careful answers. On crowded nights in the restaurant, when voices overlap and someone suddenly calls out behind her, she can feel herself leave the room for a second, the edges of things going far away. She is ashamed of how often fear organizes her day. She tells the story quietly, with long pauses, as though part of her is still trying not to be noticed. Even now, safety feels temporary, something she borrows but does not fully trust.
